mainTopic: The three-month wait before remarriage: when it starts, why it exists, why it must be three months, and the ban on marrying another man's pregnant or nursing wife
overview: This amud discusses the three-month wait before a woman may remarry. First, a ברייתא about a יבמה shows that her three months count from her husband's death, not from the חליצה. רבא defends this with a קל וחומר: if the three months already lift a כרת prohibition, they surely lift a lighter לאו. Next the גמרא asks why all other women must wait too. שמואל says it is so we can tell apart the first husband's child from the second's. רבא says it is a גזירה so the child will not later fall into ערוה. The גמרא then shows why the wait must be a full three months: shorter waits, or checking her for pregnancy, still leave doubt about who the father is. Finally, it asks why a woman already known to be pregnant or nursing may not marry another man. It tests several reasons for this, and the last one, that a pregnant woman will soon be nursing, continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The last clause of the ברייתא: after three months, no new wait
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by ruling that if the חליצה took place more than three months after the husband's death, the woman does not need to wait another three months before remarrying.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the חליצה was done after three months, she does not need to wait three months.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting the final line of the ברייתא it has been studying. This line sets up the inference the גמרא is about to draw in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא already said that a יבמה must wait three months to see if she is pregnant. Here it adds that if three months have already passed by the time of the חליצה, she can marry right away. Pay attention to this line, because the גמרא is about to learn something important from it.

keyTerms.meaning: After three [months]
To wait
Months

phrases.english: If after three months,
she does not need to wait three months.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְאַחַר שְׁלֹשָׁה אֵין צְרִיכָה לְהַמְתִּין שְׁלֹשָׁה חֳדָשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא that was quoted earlier in the sugya.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If חליצה is done more than three months after the husband's death, no new three-month wait is needed.

steps.title: Inference: the three months count from the husband's death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws a conclusion from the last clause: the three months mentioned in the ברייתא are counted from the husband's death, not from the חליצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It must be that the three months they spoke about are counted from the time the husband died, not from the time of the יבם's חליצה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is drawing a logical conclusion from the line it just quoted. Since she does not wait after a late חליצה, the clock must have started at the husband's death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the count started at the חליצה, she would always need three more months after it. The ברייתא says she does not need that, so the count must start at the husband's death. This sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: It must be / this shows that
The husband's death
The ceremony that frees a יבמה from the יבם
The brother-in-law who could do ייבום

steps.whatToRemember: For a יבמה, the three-month wait is counted from the husband's death, not from the חליצה.

phrases.english: It must be that the three months that they spoke about
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the ה in round brackets. The meaning is the same either way.

phrases.english: are counted from the time of the husband's death,
and not from the time of the yavam's ḥalitza.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a conclusion from the wording of the ברייתא's last clause.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: For a יבמה, the three months begin at the husband's death.

steps.title: Why is this different from a גט?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the inference. With a גט, both רב (from the giving) and שמואל (from the writing) count the three months from the גט itself, not from an earlier point. So why not count from the חליצה here?
steps.simpleTranslation: How is this different from a גט? There, רב said the count starts when the גט is given, and שמואל said it starts when the גט is written!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the conclusion it just reached by comparing it to divorce. With a גט, the count starts at the גט, the step that actually ends the connection.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions about a גט start the count at the גט and not earlier. The tie between a יבמה and the יבם only fully ends at the חליצה. So, by the same logic, her count should start at the חליצה and not at the death.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference?
Bill of divorce
Giving (handing over the גט)
Writing (of the גט)

phrases.english: What is different from a bill of divorce,
where Rav said: from the time of the giving,
phrases.notes: He means the three months of waiting after a divorce start when the גט is handed to her.

phrases.english: and Shmuel said: from the time of the writing!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference of step 2 by comparing it to the rules of a גט.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion that a יבמה's three months are counted from the husband's death.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With a גט, the count starts at the act that ends the marriage. The parallel act for a יבמה is the חליצה, so her count should start there.

steps.title: רבא's קל וחומר: if כרת is lifted, a לאו surely is
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers with a קל וחומר. Three months after the husband's death, we already permit the יבמה to the יבם, even though if she were pregnant he would be forbidden to her with כרת. So the lighter לאו against marrying a stranger soon after the death must surely end at the same time.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: it is a קל וחומר. You permitted a prohibition that carries כרת. A prohibition that is only a לאו should surely be permitted too!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains why the יבמה is different from a גט. The three-month count already permits a very serious prohibition, so it must also permit a lighter one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If she were pregnant, the יבם would be forbidden to her as אשת אח, which carries כרת. Yet ייבום is allowed three months after the death. If the כרת prohibition falls away from the death, then the לאו of marrying another man within three months surely falls away from the death too, not from the חליצה.

keyTerms.meaning: A reasoning from a lighter case to a stricter one (or the reverse)
A prohibition punished by כרת (spiritual cutting off)
A regular negative prohibition
All the more so

steps.whatToRemember: The count runs from the husband's death because the three months already permit the serious כרת prohibition of the יבם. The lighter לאו against marrying someone else is surely permitted from the same point.
steps.confusionAlert: The כרת here is not about the woman marrying someone else. It is about the יבם, who would be forbidden to her as אשת אח if she were pregnant. The לאו is the ban on anyone marrying her within three months.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule: a יבמה who had חליצה more than three months after her husband's death may remarry right away.

phrases.english: Rava said: It is an a fortiori inference:
a prohibition of karet you have permitted,
phrases.notes: This is the ban of אשת אח, which would forbid her to the יבם if she were pregnant. It is lifted three months after the death.

phrases.english: a prohibition of a regular negative commandment, is it not all the more so?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3 and defends the inference of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Logical distinction based on a קל וחומר
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought a יבמה is like a divorcee, so her count would start at the act that ends the bond (the חליצה).
steps.terutzMaskana: Since the three months from the death already permit the כרת prohibition with the יבם, the lighter לאו against remarrying is surely permitted from the death as well.

steps.title: Why must ordinary women wait three months?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling that all other women must also wait three months. It asks for the reason, since the יבמה's reason does not apply to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'And the same is true for all other women.' It makes sense for a יבמה, for the reason we gave. But all other women, why should they wait?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings up the next line of the משנה and asks why ordinary widows or divorcees need to wait three months. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A יבמה waits because if she is pregnant, the יבם would be marrying his brother's wife, which is forbidden. An ordinary woman marrying a stranger has no such problem. So the גמרא needs a new reason for her wait.

keyTerms.meaning: All other women: any widow or divorcee who is not a יבמה
Granted / it makes sense: the first half of a 'this I understand, but that?' question
As we said: pointing back to a reason already given
Why?

phrases.english: And similarly, all other women.
Granted, a יבמה must wait,
for the reason we said.
But all other women, why must they wait?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא יְבָמָה, כְּדַאֲמַרַן. אֶלָּא שְׁאָר כׇּל הַנָּשִׁים אַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the יבמה's waiting period to the next clause of the משנה about all other women.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason ordinary women, who face no אשת אח problem, must still wait three months.

steps.title: So we can tell which husband is the father
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן in the name of שמואל learns from a פסוק that we must be able to tell apart the first husband's child from the second husband's child.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: Because the פסוק says, 'To be a God to you and to your seed after you.' So we must be able to tell apart the seed of the first husband from the seed of the second.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives the reason for the three-month wait: so it will be clear which husband a baby belongs to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links God's closeness to a person's known children, so lineage must be clear. If a woman remarries right away and has a baby, nobody would know if it is from the first or second husband. After three months, a pregnancy from the first husband can be noticed.

keyTerms.meaning: Because the פסוק says
Your seed: your children
To distinguish, to tell apart
The first husband / the second husband

steps.whyThisMatters: This reason, keeping lineage clear, is the basis of the general rule that a woman waits three months before remarrying.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said that Shmuel said:
Because the verse says:
"To be a God to you
and to your seed after you,"
to tell apart the seed of the first husband
from the seed of the second husband.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל, מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמַר קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Women wait three months so it will be clear whether a child is from the first or the second husband, based on בראשית 17:7.

steps.title: A converted couple also waits, though the father is clear
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges שמואל from a ברייתא: a man and woman who convert together must wait three months, even though there is no question who the father is.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected: A ברייתא says, 'Therefore, a male convert and a female convert must wait three months.' Here, what is there to tell apart?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks שמואל's reason by pointing to a case where the wait applies but there is no doubt about which man is the father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The couple was married before converting and stays married afterward, so any baby is clearly from this husband. If the whole reason for waiting is to know which husband is the father, this couple should not need to wait. Yet the ברייתא says they do.

keyTerms.meaning: Therefore
A male convert and a female convert
To wait

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection:
"Therefore, a male convert and a female convert
need to wait three months."
Here, what is there to tell apart?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reason given in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's reason that the wait is to tell apart the first husband's child from the second's.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A converted couple must wait, yet there is only one man involved, so there is nothing to tell apart. The reason does not seem to fit the rule.

steps.title: Telling apart before and after the conversion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that even for the converted couple there is something to tell apart: whether the child was conceived before the conversion or after it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, there is something to tell apart: seed that was planted in holiness from seed that was not planted in holiness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל by showing that the idea of 'telling apart' still works for the converted couple.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is no longer which man is the father, but when the baby was conceived. A child conceived after the conversion was conceived as a Jew, in holiness. A child conceived before was not. The wait makes this clear, so שמואל's reason holds.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too
That was sown, conceived
In holiness: after the parents became Jewish

steps.whatToRemember: The three-month wait is about clear lineage. Usually that means which husband is the father. For a converted couple, it means whether the child was conceived before or after the conversion.

phrases.english: Here too, there is something to tell apart:
between seed that was sown in holiness
and seed that was not sown in holiness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's objection in step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Widening the principle: 'telling apart' also covers when the child was conceived, not only who the father is.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Telling apart' only means telling apart two different fathers, so a converted couple should not need to wait.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Telling apart' also includes telling apart a child conceived in holiness, after the conversion, from one conceived before it. So the converted couple must wait too.

steps.title: רבא's reason: so the child won't later stumble into forbidden relationships
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the three-month wait is a rabbinic גזירה. If people mistake who the child's father is, he could later marry his paternal sister, do יבום when he is not allowed to, or wrongly free a woman from יבום.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is a גזירה. Otherwise the child might marry his sister from his father, or do יבום with the wife of his brother from his mother. He might also release his mother to marry anyone, or free his יבמה to marry anyone.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different answer to the question of step 5: why must all women wait three months? He says the wait stops the child from getting mixed up about who his father is, which could lead him into forbidden relationships.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל the goal was simply to know whose child it is. For רבא the danger is what happens later: a child listed as the wrong man's son could marry his real father's daughter, or do יבום or חליצה based on the wrong family tree. So the wait is a fence (גזירה) against future איסורים.

keyTerms.meaning: A rabbinic decree made to protect against a possible mistake
His sister from his father (a paternal sister), forbidden to him
The wife of his brother from his mother only; יבום does not apply to her, so she stays forbidden
Literally 'to the market'; free to marry anyone
His יבמה, the widow of his childless brother

steps.confusionAlert: Only a brother from the same father can do יבום. A brother from the same mother only is still forbidden to the widow. That is why mixing up the father is so dangerous here.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a second, separate reason for the three-month wait. The rest of the sugya tests this reason against a ברייתא.

phrases.english: Rava said:
It is a decree, lest
he marry his sister from his father,
or do yibum with the wife of his brother from his mother.
Or he would release his mother to the marketplace.
phrases.notes: If the second husband dies, people would wrongly count this boy as his child. Then the mother would seem free of יבום and allowed to marry anyone.

phrases.english: Or he would exempt his yevama to the marketplace.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After שמואל's reason was challenged and defended (steps 7-8), רבא offers a different reason for the rule asked about in step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three-month wait is a rabbinic גזירה, so that confusion about who the father is will not lead the child into ערוה or into wrong rulings about יבום and חליצה.

steps.title: A ברייתא calls the wait an enactment for the child, not about forbidden relations
steps.stepSummary: רב חנניה quotes a ברייתא. It says all the other marriage bans are 'תקנת ערוה', but this three-month rule is 'תקנת ולד'. According to רבא, this one should also be 'תקנת ערוה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנניה objected: 'In all the other cases I call the ban an enactment about forbidden relations, and here it is an enactment for the child.' If רבא were right, all of them would be enactments about forbidden relations!
steps.whatsHappening: רב חנניה challenges רבא from a ברייתא. The ברייתא treats the three-month wait as a different kind of rule from all the others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists the bans as two types: most protect against ערוה, and this one protects the child. רבא's reason is about the child ending up in ערוה, which would make this ban the same type as the others. So the ברייתא's split seems to go against רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: An enactment made to prevent forbidden relations
An enactment made for the good of the child
'And if it were so', meaning if your view were correct

phrases.english: Rav Chananya objected:
In all of them I describe them
phrases.notes: 'All of them' means the other cases where the חכמים forbid a woman to marry or to do יבום.

phrases.english: as due to an enactment about forbidden relations,
and here as due to an enactment for the child.
And if it is so,
phrases.notes: He means: if רבא's reason were right.

phrases.english: all of them would be due to an enactment about forbidden relations!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's reason from step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the wait exists to prevent the child from coming to ערוה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא sets the three-month rule apart as תקנת ולד, unlike the other bans, which are תקנת ערוה. Under רבא it would be just another תקנת ערוה, so the ברייתא's split would make no sense.

steps.title: 'For the child' means: so the child won't run into forbidden relations
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that 'תקנת ולד' in the ברייתא means an enactment so that the child will not come to ערוה. That fits רבא exactly.
steps.simpleTranslation: This 'enactment for the child' means: so that forbidden relations will not happen to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבא. It reads the ברייתא's phrase 'for the child' as meaning 'to protect the child from forbidden relations'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that 'תקנת ולד' and 'תקנת ערוה' are opposites. The answer shows they can overlap. The other bans protect the people marrying now, while this one protects the child later on. So the ברייתא still has a reason to list it separately, and רבא's reason stands.

keyTerms.meaning: So that he should not encounter or run into

steps.whatToRemember: There are two reasons for the three-month wait. שמואל says it is to tell apart the two husbands' children. רבא says it is a גזירה so the child won't later fall into ערוה, and in his view 'תקנת ולד' means protecting the child from that.

phrases.english: This 'due to an enactment for the child'
means that forbidden relations should not happen to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב חנניה's objection by reinterpreting the ברייתא's wording.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'תקנת ולד' means something other than preventing ערוה, so it is the opposite of 'תקנת ערוה'.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'תקנת ולד' means protecting the child himself from ערוה, which matches רבא's גזירה.

steps.title: Why not wait only one month?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא agrees a two-month wait would leave doubt, but asks why a one-month wait would not be enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that she can't wait only two months, because then a baby born seven months after the new marriage could be a nine-month baby from the first husband or a seven-month baby from the second. But let her wait only one month! If she gives birth after seven months, the baby is a seven-month baby from the second husband. If she gives birth after eight months, the baby is a nine-month baby from the first husband.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the waiting period has to be a full three months. It agrees two months is too short, but argues that one month should already let us tell who the father is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question works on an assumption: a baby born in its seventh or ninth month can live, but a baby born in its eighth month cannot. With a one-month wait, a birth seven months after the new marriage fits only the second husband. A birth eight months after it fits only the first husband, as a nine-month baby. So it seems there would be no doubt, and three months would be more than we need.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense (we agree with this part, but...)
A baby born after nine months of pregnancy
A baby born after seven months of pregnancy
The first husband / the second (later) husband

steps.confusionAlert: All the counting of months here starts from the new marriage, not from conception. 'After eight months' means eight months after the second wedding. With a one-month wait, that is nine months after the first husband.

phrases.english: It makes sense that she should wait two months
and then marry — no, that is not enough,
because that is a case of doubt:
maybe the baby is a nine-month baby of the first husband,
or maybe it is a seven-month baby of the second husband.
But let her wait one month and then marry,
and if she gives birth seven months later —
this is a seven-month baby of the second husband.
And if she gives birth eight months later —
phrases.notes: The גמרא is assuming a baby born in its eighth month can't survive, so a living baby here can't be an eight-month baby.

phrases.english: this is a nine-month baby of the first husband!

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא תַּמְתִּין שְׁנֵי חֳדָשִׁים וְתִנָּשֵׂא — לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After discussing the reasons for the wait (שמואל: to tell apart the two husbands' children; רבא: a גזירה against future ערוה), the גמרא now asks why the period must be exactly three months.
steps.kashyaTarget: The length of the three-month waiting period
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Because eight-month babies are not viable, a one-month wait already lets us tell the fathers apart. So three months seems unnecessary.

steps.title: She may have conceived a month after the second marriage
steps.stepSummary: Even a birth eight months after the second marriage could be from the second husband, since she may have conceived only a month into that marriage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if she gives birth eight months later, you could say the baby is from the second husband. Maybe she waited a month into the marriage and only then became pregnant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: a one-month wait does not remove the doubt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed pregnancy starts right at the second wedding. But conception can happen later. If she became pregnant a month after the wedding, a birth eight months after the wedding is really a seven-month baby, and that baby can live. So a living baby born then could be from either husband, and the doubt comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: She was delayed (she waited some time before becoming pregnant)
She became pregnant
One could say

phrases.english: Even if she gives birth eight months later,
one could say that the baby is the second husband's.
Perhaps she went one month into the marriage first
and only then became pregnant.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי לִתְמָנְיָא יָלְדָה, אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר דְּבָתְרָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12 by showing that a one-month wait leaves the doubt in place.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects a hidden assumption: conception does not have to happen right at the wedding
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With a one-month wait, a birth eight months into the second marriage can only be a nine-month baby of the first husband.
steps.terutzMaskana: Conception may come later, so that birth could be a seven-month baby of the second husband. The doubt stays.

steps.title: Why not wait two and a half months?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes again: a wait of two and a half months seems to remove the doubt completely, so why require three?
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let her wait two and a half months and marry. If she gives birth seven months later, it is a seven-month baby of the second husband. If she gives birth six and a half months later, it is a nine-month baby of the first husband. If it were the second husband's baby, it would be only six and a half months old, and such a baby cannot live!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new, sharper question about the length of the wait. The next step answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the plan uses the fact that a baby born at six and a half months cannot live. With a two-and-a-half-month wait, a living baby born six and a half months after the second wedding has to be a nine-month baby of the first husband. A birth at seven months fits the second husband. So it seems two and a half months already settles everything, and the extra half month needs an explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: And a half
Six and a half (months)
Does not survive

steps.confusionAlert: This step is only the question. The answer, based on מר זוטרא, comes in the next step.

phrases.english: But let her wait two and a half months and then marry,
for if she gives birth seven months later —
this is a seven-month baby of the second husband,
and if she gives birth six and a half months later —
this is a nine-month baby of the first husband.
Because if it were the second husband's baby —
a six-and-a-half-month baby does not survive!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The one-month idea was rejected in step 13, so the גמרא tries a waiting period closer to three months.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for a full three months instead of two and a half
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A six-and-a-half-month baby cannot live, so with a two-and-a-half-month wait every birth can be matched to one husband. The extra half month seems unneeded.

steps.title: Even two and a half months leaves doubt
steps.stepSummary: A baby born six and a half months after the second marriage could belong to either husband, because a seven-month baby can be born before the seventh month is complete.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if she gave birth six and a half months into the second marriage, one could say the baby belongs to the second husband. As מר זוטרא said: even the opinion that a nine-month baby is born only after full months agrees that a seven-month baby can be born after incomplete months.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 14. It shows that even a wait of two and a half months would still leave us unsure which husband is the father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Say she waited two and a half months and gave birth six and a half months after the second wedding. That is nine months after the first husband, so the baby could be his full-term child. But it could also be a seven-month baby from the second husband, born early in the seventh month. Only a full three-month wait removes every doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: Six and a half (months)
The latter one, here the second husband
Incomplete months, a birth before the month count is full

phrases.english: Even if she gave birth after six and a half months,
one could say that the baby is from the latter husband,
as Mar Zutra said:
Even according to the one who says a woman who gives birth at nine months
does not give birth after incomplete months,
a woman who gives birth at seven months can give birth after incomplete months.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי לְשִׁיתָּא וּפַלְגָא יָלְדָה, אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר דְּבָתְרָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 14's question about why two and a half months is not enough.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the doubt still exists, using a fact about early births
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A wait of two and a half months removes all doubt about the father.
steps.terutzMaskana: A seven-month baby can be born after six and a half months, so only a full three months removes the doubt.

steps.title: The source: the birth of שמואל הנביא
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק about חנה giving birth to שמואל shows that a baby can be born after six months and two days.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'And it came to pass, at the turnings of the days.' The fewest 'turnings' is two, and the fewest 'days' is two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to back up מר זוטרא's claim that a baby can be born early in the seventh month.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each season, or 'turning,' of the year is three months, so two seasons make six months. The plural word 'days' means at least two days. So שמואל was born six months and two days after he was conceived, which proves a live birth can come after incomplete months.

keyTerms.meaning: Seasons, the turnings of the year, three months each
The smallest number a plural word can mean, which is two

steps.whyThisMatters: This early-birth fact is the reason the waiting period must be a full three months and not less.

phrases.english: As it is stated: 'And it came to pass, at the turnings of the days',
phrases.notes: שמואל א 1:20, about חנה giving birth to שמואל.

phrases.english: the fewest 'seasons' can mean is two,
phrases.notes: Two seasons of three months each come to six months.

phrases.english: and the fewest 'days' can mean is two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source from a פסוק for מר זוטרא's claim in step 15.
steps.raayaObject: That a seven-month baby can be born after incomplete months
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק in שמואל א about the birth of שמואל

steps.title: Why not marry quickly and check her later?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests she wait only a short time, marry, and then be checked for pregnancy once three months have passed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let her wait a little and then marry, and when three months have passed, let us examine her!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests an easier plan that would make the long wait unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pregnancy starts to show at about three months. If she is visibly pregnant three months after her first marriage ended, the baby must be from the first husband. So why not let her remarry right away and settle the question with a check?

keyTerms.meaning: A tiny amount, any short time
To examine her body for signs of pregnancy

phrases.english: But let her wait a short while and marry,
and when three months are complete, let us examine her!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַמְתִּין מַשֶּׁהוּ וְתִנָּשֵׂא, וְכִי מָלוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה חֳדָשִׁים לִבְדְּקַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that three months has been justified, the גמרא asks why we need a waiting period at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for a full three-month wait before remarrying
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A physical check at three months could settle who the father is without making her wait.

steps.title: רב ספרא: we do not examine married women
steps.stepSummary: Examining a married woman's body would make her repulsive to her husband, so the check is not allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said: We do not examine married women, so they will not become repulsive to their husbands.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא rejects the plan from step 17.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea of a check works in theory, but it cannot be done in practice. Inspecting her body would shame her and could make her husband find her repulsive. So the waiting period stays.

keyTerms.meaning: Married women
Become repulsive or shamed

phrases.english: Rav Safra said:
One does not examine married women,
so that they will not become repulsive to their husbands.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב סָפְרָא: אֵין בּוֹדְקִין אֶת הַנְּשׂוּאוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 17 by showing the proposed check is not allowed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical objection: the solution would cause shame
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A physical check at three months could replace the waiting period.
steps.terutzMaskana: Married women are not examined, so the check is not an option.

steps.title: Then check the way she walks
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests checking her without touching her, by watching how she walks.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us examine her by the way she walks!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב ספרא with a gentler kind of check, setting up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ספרא's problem was the shame of a physical exam. Watching how she walks involves no exam at all, since a woman three months pregnant walks differently. So the shame problem seems to disappear, and the question of why she must wait comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: Her way of walking

phrases.english: But let us examine her by the way she walks!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב ספרא's answer by offering a check that brings no shame.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ספרא's reason that checking is not possible
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Watching her walk avoids any physical exam, so it brings no shame and could still reveal a pregnancy.

steps.title: A woman might hide her pregnancy on purpose
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא rejects the walking test, because a woman may hide her pregnancy so her child will inherit from her new husband.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא said: A woman may hide her pregnancy so that her son will inherit her husband's property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the suggestion from Step 19 to check her by watching how she walks. That check can't be trusted, because she may walk carefully to hide that she is pregnant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A woman pregnant from her first husband may want the child to be seen as the new husband's son, so the baby will inherit from him. Since she has a reason to hide the pregnancy, watching her walk proves nothing. So the full three-month wait stays.

keyTerms.meaning: Covers or hides herself, meaning she hides her pregnancy
Her husband's property

steps.whatToRemember: No shortcut works, so the woman must wait the full three months before remarrying.

phrases.english: Rami bar Ḥama said:
A woman covers herself up,
phrases.notes: He means she walks in a way that hides her pregnancy, so watching her walk tells us nothing.

phrases.english: so that her son will inherit
her husband's property.
phrases.notes: This means the new husband's property.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר חָמָא: אִשָּׁה מְחַפָּה עַצְמָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the suggestion in Step 19 by showing that the walking test can't be relied on.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical: the test can be fooled on purpose
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Watching how she walks could show whether she is pregnant, so she would not need to wait.
steps.terutzMaskana: She may hide the pregnancy on purpose, so the full three-month wait is needed.

steps.title: If she is clearly pregnant, why can't she marry right away?
steps.stepSummary: If we already know she is pregnant, the reason for waiting is gone, yet a ברייתא forbids marrying another man's pregnant or nursing wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: When we know for sure that she is pregnant, let her marry right away! So why does a ברייתא teach: A man may not marry a woman pregnant with another man's child, or nursing another man's child, and if he did marry her, he must divorce her and may never take her back?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. The three-month wait is there to find out whether she is pregnant, so if we already know she is, she should be allowed to marry at once. But a ברייתא says she may not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason for the wait is to know who the father is. When the pregnancy is already obvious, there is no doubt about the father. Even so, the ברייתא forbids the marriage, and the penalty is very strong: divorce, with no chance to remarry ever. So there must be some other reason behind it.

keyTerms.meaning: We know for certain
A woman pregnant with another man's child
A woman nursing another man's child
He may never take her back

phrases.english: Where we know for certain
that she is pregnant, let her marry!
Why is it taught in a baraita:
A man may not marry a woman pregnant by another man
or a woman nursing another man's child.
And if he married her, he must divorce her
and may never take her back!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכָא דְּקִים לַן דִּמְעוּבֶּרֶת הִיא, תִּנָּשֵׂא! אַלְּמָה תַּנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the wait is settled as being about finding a pregnancy, the גמרא asks about a case where the pregnancy is already known.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא that forbids marrying a woman pregnant with another man's child
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the only purpose of waiting is to know who the father is, a known pregnancy leaves no doubt, so the ban needs another reason.

steps.title: A safety rule to protect the baby
steps.stepSummary: The ban is a גזירה, out of fear that a new pregnancy could crush the baby she is already carrying.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a rabbinic decree, out of fear that her baby will be made into a sandal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that the ban has nothing to do with knowing who the father is. It is a safety rule to protect the baby inside her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fear is that relations could lead to a second pregnancy, which might press on the first baby and leave it flat and misshapen, like a סנדל fish. The חכמים made a גזירה to prevent that harm.

keyTerms.meaning: A safety rule the חכמים made to prevent a problem
Her baby before birth
A flat, misshapen fetus, shaped like a סנדל fish

phrases.english: It is a decree, lest her fetus become a sandal.
phrases.notes: A סנדל here is a flat, misshapen fetus, named after a flat fish. The worry is that a second pregnancy squashes the first baby.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new reason for the ברייתא's ban, one that is not about knowing who the father is.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ban only makes sense if it is about knowing who the father is.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban is a rabbinic safety rule to protect the baby from harm.

steps.title: Shouldn't the same worry apply to his own pregnant wife?
steps.stepSummary: If the fear is harm to the baby, a husband should also be forbidden to be with his own pregnant wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the same should apply to his own wife!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer in Step 22. The danger to the baby should be the same when a husband is with his own pregnant wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A safety worry should not depend on who the father is. So if the danger is real, a man should be kept away from his own pregnant wife too, and we never hear of such a rule.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
His own as well

phrases.english: If so, his own as well!
phrases.notes: He means his own wife who is pregnant with his own child.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason given in Step 22 by applying it to a man's own pregnant wife.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason that the ban protects the baby
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The danger is the same no matter who the father is, so the reason seems to prove too much.

steps.title: With his own wife: use a מוך, or trust Heaven
steps.stepSummary: With his own pregnant wife, the problem is handled either by using a מוך or by trusting that Heaven will protect them, depending on which opinion you follow.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the one who says a מוך is used, she uses a מוך. And according to the one who says Heaven will have mercy, Heaven will have mercy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how a husband and his own pregnant wife deal with the danger. It uses two known opinions about women for whom pregnancy is dangerous.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Elsewhere there is a מחלוקת about women in danger from pregnancy. One opinion says she uses a מוך, an absorbent pad that prevents pregnancy. The other says she lives normally and מן השמים ירחמו, Heaven will protect her. Whichever opinion you follow also applies to his own pregnant wife, so she is not forbidden to him.

keyTerms.meaning: A soft absorbent pad used to prevent pregnancy
Heaven will have mercy and protect her
According to the one who says

phrases.english: If according to the one who says with a resorbent, then with a resorbent,
phrases.notes: This points to a known argument about women for whom pregnancy is dangerous. One view lets them use a מוך to prevent pregnancy.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לְמַאן דְּאָמַר מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם יְרַחֲמוּ —
phrases.english: and if according to the one who says Heaven will have mercy,
then Heaven will have mercy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 23 by showing that his own pregnant wife is covered by an existing approach to the danger.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Using an existing מחלוקת to cover the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: His own pregnant wife should be forbidden to him because of the danger.
steps.terutzMaskana: With his own wife, the danger is handled by a מוך or by trusting Heaven, depending on the opinion.

steps.title: The same solutions should work for another man's pregnant wife
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that the solutions used for a man's own pregnant wife, a מוך or trusting Heaven, should also work when he marries another man's pregnant wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too: if you follow the opinion that says 'with a מוך,' then use a מוך. If you follow the opinion that says 'Heaven will have mercy,' then Heaven will have mercy!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reason given in step 22. The fear of crushing the baby was solved for a man's own wife, so the same solution should work for another man's wife too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 24 used a מוך or 'Heaven will protect' to allow relations with one's own pregnant wife. Whatever protects the baby there should protect it here as well. So the worry about crushing the baby cannot explain why marrying another man's pregnant wife is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too: the same logic applies to this case
If
According to the one who says
An absorbent cloth used to prevent pregnancy
Heaven will have mercy: trusting that God will protect them

phrases.english: Here too:
phrases.notes: 'Here' means marrying another man's pregnant wife.

phrases.english: if according to the one who says 'with a מוך,' then with a מוך;

phrases.aramaic: אִי לְמַאן דְּאָמַר מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם יְרַחֲמוּ —
phrases.english: if according to the one who says 'Heaven will have mercy,'
then Heaven will have mercy!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא נָמֵי: אִי לְמַאן דְּאָמַר בְּמוֹךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the answer of step 24 and applies it to the case of step 22, which undoes that reason.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason in step 22: a new pregnancy could crush the baby already there.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a מוך or Heaven's protection removes the danger for a man's own pregnant wife, it removes the same danger for another man's pregnant wife. So there is no reason left for the ban.

steps.title: A new reason: pressure on the baby
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the old reason and suggests that the ban is because of דחסה, pressure on the baby during relations.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the reason is because of pressure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up on the 'crushing by a new pregnancy' reason and offers a new one. The physical pressure of relations could harm the baby.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מוך only prevents a new pregnancy, and the old worry was about a new pregnancy. The new worry is the pressure of relations itself, which a מוך does not prevent. So step 25's challenge does not touch this reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather: dropping the old answer for a new one
Because of
Pressure: physical pressing on the baby during relations

phrases.english: Rather, it is because of pressure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the reason that step 25 knocked down.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing the reason with a new one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ban was about a second pregnancy crushing the baby, which a מוך could solve.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban is about the pressure of relations itself, which a מוך does not solve.

steps.title: Then his own pregnant wife should be forbidden too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if pressure is the problem, a man should not be allowed to be with his own pregnant wife either.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, his own wife should also be forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new reason of דחסה. Pressure on the baby happens just as much when the baby is his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pressure is a physical fact, and it does not matter who the father is. Yet a man is allowed to be with his own pregnant wife. So the pressure reason seems to prove too much.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: if that reason is true
His own (wife or child)
Also, too

phrases.english: If so, his own as well!
phrases.notes: He means: if he's with his own pregnant wife, the same pressure would harm his own baby.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the new reason from step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reason of דחסה in step 26.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Pressure harms any baby, so a man's own pregnant wife should be forbidden too. But she is permitted.

steps.title: A father is careful with his own baby
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a man has mercy on his own baby and will be careful not to press too hard.
steps.simpleTranslation: With his own, he has mercy on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the pressure reason. A father cares about his own unborn child, so he will be gentle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference is not physical but emotional. A father naturally protects his own baby, so there is no real danger with his own wife. With another man's baby, he might not be as careful.

keyTerms.meaning: He has mercy, he takes care
Upon it (the baby)

phrases.english: His own: he has mercy on it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 27 by showing how his own wife is different.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a difference between the two cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Pressure endangers his own baby just as much, so his own wife should be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: A father's mercy on his own child keeps him careful, so there is no danger with his own wife.

steps.title: He would be careful with another man's baby too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: a man would also have mercy on another man's baby and be careful.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, he has mercy on it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the answer of step 28. Any decent person would take care not to hurt a baby, even one that is not his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not accept that a man would carelessly harm another man's unborn child. So the difference between his own baby and another man's baby falls apart. Because of that, the pressure reason cannot explain the ban.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: the case of another man's baby

phrases.english: Here too: he has mercy on it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the answer of step 28 against itself, which knocks down the reason of step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The difference given in step 28 between one's own baby and another man's baby.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Mercy on a baby is not limited to the father. A man would be careful with any baby, so the pressure danger is equally small in both cases.

steps.title: A new reason: a pregnant woman will soon be nursing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a new reason: a typical pregnant woman is about to become a nursing mother.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, an ordinary pregnant woman stands ready to become a nursing mother.
steps.whatsHappening: After both earlier reasons fell, the גמרא starts a brand-new explanation. This line is a setup, and the full reason continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of focusing on danger during the pregnancy, the גמרא looks ahead to what happens after birth. A pregnant woman will soon be nursing. That connects the ban on a pregnant woman to the ban on a nursing woman, which comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Ordinary, typical, the usual case
A pregnant woman
A nursing woman
Stands, is set to (become)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the end of the answer. The גמרא will explain in the next lines why being a future nursing mother matters.

phrases.english: Rather: an ordinary pregnant woman stands to become a nursing woman,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the pressure reason that step 29 knocked down.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replacing the reason with a new one
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ban on a pregnant woman is about harm to the baby during the pregnancy.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban is about the fact that she will soon be nursing; the full explanation follows.
